thread.title: Stock Buyback Spending Could Boost Stock Market Outlook In 2019 — But How Much?

author: SCOTT LEHTONEN
title: Stock Buyback Spending Could Boost Stock Market Outlook In 2019 — But How Much?
text:
Stock buyback programs had their biggest year ever in 2018. But can they come to the rescue in 2019 as stocks struggle to break free from the throes of the recent bear market?
X The stock market needs all the help it can get as it faces a confluence of potential issues: a lingering trade war , rising interest rates and a slowing global economy.
Stock buyback, or share repurchase, programs occur when a company buys back its own shares from the marketplace. The company's goal is to reduce the number of outstanding shares, increasing the value of each remaining share.
Last year, companies used funds from President Trump's corporate tax cuts to buy back a record number of their own shares. That helped boost share prices until the stock market peaked in September. But will companies continue to be aggressive buyers of their own shares after the Nasdaq and S&P 500 fell as much as 24% from their highs? (Read The Big Picture daily to stay in sync with stock market trends.)
 Howard Silverblatt, senior index analyst at S&P Dow Jones Indices, says lower stock prices will increase the effectiveness of a potential stock buyback. Lower stock prices "would increase the number of shares a company can buy with the same expenditure and further increase the EPS tail wind," he said.
Most analysts agree that stock buyback levels in 2019 will be similar to last year. With stock market volatility back on the rise, stock buybacks could be a steadying force in a sea of volatility. (Learn how to invest after a stock market correction .)
Impact Of Trump Tax Cuts Trump signed the Tax Cuts And Jobs Act on Dec. 22, 2017. The tax law cut the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%, the lowest since 1939. It also allowed companies to repatriate $2.6 trillion held in foreign cash stockpiles, paying a one-time tax rate of 15.5% on the cash transfers.
The tax plan left many companies, particularly large-cap global firms, with strong reserves of cash. Some companies increased wages or handed out bonuses, including insurance company Aflac ( AFL ), American Airlines ( AAL ) and shipping giant FedEx ( FDX ). Others put that cash to use in the form of extensive buyback programs, rewarding shareholders with boosted stock prices.
According to data from S&P Dow Jones Indices, stock buybacks by companies in the S&P 500 index climbed to $720.4 billion in the 12 months ended in September 2018, with about $203 billion in Q3 2018 alone. While end of the year figures have yet to be finalized, Silverblatt says it was a record year. Investment research firm TrimTab says U.S. companies spent $1 trillion.
Stock buybacks totaled $519.4 billion in 2017 and $536.38 billion in 2016. The previous record was held in 2007, when companies spent $589.1 billion.
Why Do Companies Buy Back Stock? The reasons why companies buy back stock start with share value. A company's management feels the stock price is undervalued relative to its fundamentals, and higher stock prices are ahead.
Another potential reason for a stock buyback is excess cash. After fulfilling its investment opportunities, a company that still has lots of cash on hand may choose to return some of that cash to shareholders.
These buybacks can provide a steady flow of demand for a stock that may not have other compelling growth catalysts.
Since 2013, for example, Dow Jones industrials component Microsoft ( MSFT ) saw its stock price continue to move higher despite single-digit revenue growth in 2013 and 2015 and a 9% decline in 2016. After nine consecutive quarters of single-digit or negative sales growth, revenue grew 13% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2017 and has yet to fall back into the single digits.
During that time, Microsoft consistently bought back its shares each quarter. Shares are trading about 11% off their all-time highs and have surged more than 280% since the beginning of 2013, easily beating the S&P 500's 80% gain.
Legendary investor Warren Buffett believes that buybacks, when done at the right prices and for the right reasons, can be the most effective use of corporate capital. But at the 2016 Berkshire Hathaway ( BRKB ) annual meeting, Buffett cautioned that companies should be cognizant of valuation. "It's gotten quite common," he said, "to buy back stock at very high prices that don't do the shareholders any good at all."
On the downside, a stock price can go much lower than the company ever anticipates.
Check out former Dow Jones stock General Electric ( GE ) over the past few years. Former CEO Jeff Immelt spent $21 billion in 2016 buying back GE shares at an average price of 30.30. Yet GE shares are trading around 8 per share in the stock market today , about 75% off the 33 high set in July 2016.
A surprise loser of recent buybacks was Apple ( AAPL ). According to the Wall Street Journal , Apple lost about $9 billion in 2018 as a result of buying its own stock. That loss magnified on Jan. 3 when Apple's slashed earnings outlook took the iPhone maker's stock down 10%.
Is The Stock Market Correction A Buying Opportunity? Though they were credited as a reason for the market's continued ascent in 2018, buybacks — or lack thereof — may have contributed to the stock market's sharp sell-off in October. That sell-off coincided with the third quarter earnings season, which created a "buyback blackout period."
Leading up to their earnings releases, companies face greater restrictions on buying back stock to avoid the appearance of using inside information. The unofficial blackout period generally goes from the last two weeks of a quarter until after earnings are announced.
With the December pullback in stocks to bear market territory for the S&P and tech-heavy Nasdaq, companies may be poised to put some of their authorized capital to work. Indeed, a number of companies set in motion huge stock buyback plans even as the stock market crumpled in December.
December 2018 Stock Buyback List Among the companies announcing stock buybacks were:
Boeing ( BA ). On Dec. 10, Boeing announced an $18 billion repurchase program along with a 20% dividend hike. Facebook ( FB ). On Dec. 7, the social media giant said it plans to buy back $9 billion of its own shares. The $9 billion is in addition to an existing $15 billion share repurchase program started in 2017. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ). On Dec. 18, JNJ announced a $5 billion stock buyback in response to the stock's dramatic fall driven by a Reuters report that said the company knew about asbestos in its baby power. Lowe's ( LOW ). The home improvement retailer announced a $10 billion stock buyback program Dec. 12. Pfizer ( PFE ). The drugmaker authorized a new $10 billion share repurchase program and raised its quarterly dividend Dec. 14. Stock Buyback Outlook For 2019 Many analysts see another strong year for stock buybacks, but most estimates fall just short of 2018's record spending spree.
Silverblatt estimates that the dollar amount of stock buybacks will be similar to 2018. As long as the tax structure remains the same and the economy doesn't fall apart, he expects companies will have the cash flow to fund the buybacks.
JPMorgan recently estimated $800 billion worth of buybacks will take place in 2019 due to increased profits and continued cash repatriation from the Trump tax law. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs forecast $940 billion worth of buybacks for 2019.
Joseph P. Quinlan, head of market strategy at Bank of America, said last year's record share repurchases are likely to be a one-off event. Instead, he sees lower stock buybacks as a result of decreased repatriation cash flows. "As the cost of capital continues to rise," he said, "firms will probably resort to more holding of cash/capital (in 2019) vs. doling it back to shareholders via buybacks and dividends."
Interest rates are a factor to watch. While interest rates remain historically low, increased rates raise the cost of capital and could force companies to hold onto their cash. The Fed is ready "to adjust policy quickly and flexibly" depending on the financial markets.
If investors are betting on further company stock buybacks to stem the stock market's slide, they may not have to. The stock market is already up more than 10% from its December lows, helped considerably by the Fed's reassurance. If Fed policymakers are indeed flexible in 2019, they may help coax the market higher.
